title: This Hormone May Explain Why Exercise Helps the Brain
paragraphs: We know that exercise is good for the brain. But scientists are still trying to understand exactly why. Now, a new study suggests that a hormone called irisin may be part of the answer.

Irisin is a hormone that muscles release when we are physically active. It is sometimes called the "exercise hormone," and it has been linked to metabolism and brain health. Earlier research on mice found that when mice could not produce irisin, exercise no longer improved their thinking skills.

The new study was published in the Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research in 2026. It involved 30 healthy adults over the age of 65. Of these, 24 people did a 12-week weight training program. They lifted heavy weights three times a week. The other six people continued their normal activities.

The researchers measured the amount of irisin in the participants' blood before and after their workouts. They did this during the first training session and again during the last session. They also tested the participants' memory and their ability to think of words quickly.

The results showed that after the first workout, the participants' irisin levels rose clearly. However, after 12 weeks of training, the same workout caused a smaller rise in irisin. Also, the participants' irisin levels when resting did not increase during the program.
Even so, the participants' ability to think of words improved after the training. In addition, changes in their memory were linked to how high their irisin levels rose after exercise.
Based on these results, some experts suggest that short rises in irisin after each workout may be more important for the brain than having high levels all the time.
However, the study was small, and all the participants were healthy older adults. More research is needed to see if the results are the same in younger people and over longer periods.
